title: Larger crustal earthquakes in Japan and southern California mostly started at mid-depth of local seismicity, with an excess in the deepest tenth (JMA 1998-2024, SCSN 1981-2025)
abstract: We tested if larger crustal earthquakes start deeper in the local seismogenic layer than smaller ones, after we remove differences between regions. For each event, we calculated its local depth rank p: the share of other events in the same 10 km map cell that are shallower. We removed the event's own sequence from its reference with Gardner-Knopoff time windows. We used 174,416 onshore crustal events (Mj 1.5 or more, 1998-2024) from the JMA catalog and 262,271 events (M 1.5 or more, 1981-2025) from the SCSN relocated catalog of southern California. Events of M 5 or more did not start near the base: the mean rank was 0.53 in Japan (95% cell-bootstrap interval 0.47-0.59, 164 events) and 0.59 in California (0.51-0.66, 94 events), and the median hypocentre was 1.5-1.8 km above the local D90. But the deepest tenth had an excess of larger events and the shallowest tenth did not: in Japan, 17.6% of Mj 3.5-4.5 events had p > 0.9 against 10.6% with p < 0.1 (difference +6.9 points, +3.7 to +10.1; both halves of the period agree). In California, the excess started at M 4.5 (24.1% against 12.2%; +11.9 points, +5.4 to +18.6). The small-event depth-size link was regional. In Japan, the mean rank increased by 0.023 per magnitude unit (0.013-0.032; permutation null -0.002), and the b-value of the locally deepest fifth was 0.079 lower than that of the shallowest fifth (-0.111 to -0.047), but only in cells with a D90 deeper than 10.2 km. In California, there was no clear rank increase for M 2.0-4.5 and no b decrease with relative depth. A pooled absolute-depth b decrease in Japan partly comes from a regional mix: cells with a deep D90 had a lower b at all depths, and among independent events this regional difference disappeared. Limitations: few events of M 6 or more (27 and 11); JMA velocity and displacement magnitudes rank differently at the same Mj, so a part of the Japanese effect at Mj 3-4.5 can come from the magnitude scale; the California large-event test uses mixed location types. Code, aggregate tables, figures and a hash-checked retrieval script are included; the raw catalogs are not bundled.

display.caption: Mean local depth rank p (0 = shallowest, 1 = deepest event in the same 10 km map cell) by magnitude bin, for onshore Japanese crust (JMA 1998-2024) and southern California (SCSN relocated 1981-2025). Blue: all years; orange and green: early and late halves. Bars: 95% cell-bootstrap intervals. Grey band: 95% range of a within-cell magnitude permutation null. Large events had mean ranks of 0.52-0.62, far below the local D90 (rank 0.9).

Share of events in the deepest tenth (p > 0.9, coloured) and the shallowest tenth (p < 0.1, open grey) of the local depth distribution, by magnitude group. The expected share is 0.10. The deep tail rose above 0.10 at Mj 3.5-4.5 in Japan and at M 4.5 or more in California; the shallow tail did not, so random location error does not explain the excess.

b-value (M 2.0 or more) by absolute depth (top) and by local depth rank quintile (bottom), for Japan (left) and southern California GrowClust solutions (right). Black: all cells; coloured: terciles of the cell D90. In Japan, b decreased in the locally deepest fifth only in cells with a deep D90; in California, b did not decrease with relative depth.

citations.reason: We reuse its JMA parser and hash list, and we extend its secondary test of mainshock depth relative to background seismicity to the full magnitude range and to southern California.

Das and Scholz (1983) argue that large earthquakes nucleate near the base of the seismogenic layer; most M 5 or larger events here started at mid-depth.
